req1: CT brain first to exclude a stroke
Every minute above 40 C increases organ damage. Cooling starts before imaging, and the core temperature tells you what this is.
Use a tympanic thermometer to check the temperature
Tympanic and oral readings underestimate core temperature. Use a rectal or oesophageal probe.
req2: Paracetamol and a fan, then reassess in an hour
Antipyretics do not work in heat stroke because the hypothalamic set point is normal. Cool actively and fast.
Keep cooling until the temperature reaches 36 C
Overshoot causes hypothermia. Stop active cooling at about 38.5 C.
req3: Chlorpromazine for shivering
Antipsychotics lower the seizure threshold and impair thermoregulation. Use a benzodiazepine.
Skip glucose, he is not diabetic
Hypoglycaemia occurs in heat stroke and causes seizures and confusion. Check it.
req4: Restrict fluids because of his hypertension
Rhabdomyolysis needs high volume fluid to protect the kidneys. Monitor urine output closely.
Give potassium chloride for the weakness
Rhabdomyolysis causes hyperkalaemia. Adding potassium can be fatal.
req5: Discharge after cooling if he wakes up
Heat stroke causes delayed liver failure, coagulopathy and kidney injury. He needs ICU monitoring.
Give paracetamol regularly for comfort
Liver injury is common after heat stroke. Avoid hepatotoxic drugs.

req1: Treat the haemoptysis as tuberculosis and isolate
The exposure history points to leptospirosis with pulmonary haemorrhage. Oxygen and early recognition come first.
Give oxygen only if saturation falls below 85%
Pulmonary haemorrhage deteriorates fast. Give high flow oxygen now and prepare for escalation.
req2: Wait for leptospira serology to confirm before antibiotics
Serology takes days and is often negative early. Start antibiotics on clinical suspicion.
Oral amoxicillin as an outpatient
Severe leptospirosis with jaundice and haemoptysis needs IV ceftriaxone or penicillin and admission.
req3: Large fluid boluses to flush the kidneys
Fluid overload worsens pulmonary haemorrhage. Give careful boluses with reassessment.
Hold potassium, the kidneys are failing
Leptospirosis often causes a non-oliguric hypokalaemic kidney injury. Check and replace potassium.
req4: Admit to the general ward and recheck in the morning
He is deteriorating with respiratory failure and kidney injury. He needs ICU and renal replacement.
High dose steroids as primary treatment
Steroids are not proven for leptospirosis pulmonary haemorrhage. Supportive ICU care and dialysis are the mainstays.
req5: Treat the patient and leave public health to others
Leptospirosis is notifiable and others in the village share the exposure. Notify and advise.
Give every villager doxycycline for a month
Prophylaxis is for high risk exposed workers, not everyone. Notify and target advice.

req1: Reassure her without examining the lump
Reassurance without examination is not credible and may miss pathology. Examine properly.
Order an urgent CT neck tonight
She already has imaging. Examine for red flags and review the existing scan.
req2: Book the PET-CT to put her mind at rest
Imaging without indication rarely reassures and can reveal incidental findings that cause more harm.
Refer for an excisional biopsy
A small mobile node without red flags does not justify biopsy. Explain the reasoning instead.
req3: Tell her to come back to the emergency department if she is worried
That reinforces emergency visits. Give a defined outpatient plan with an endpoint.
Arrange ultrasound every week to monitor the node
Repeated imaging fuels checking. A single repeat at 6 weeks if it persists is enough.
req4: Prescribe diazepam for the anxiety
Benzodiazepines from the emergency department risk dependence and do not treat health anxiety.
Ignore the anxiety, it is not an emergency problem
Health anxiety drives repeat attendance. Offering help addresses the real problem.

req1: Keep the compression garment on to tamponade the bleeding
The garment hides the swelling and can impair perfusion. Remove it and examine.
Phone the clinic for advice before examining
She is faint after surgery. Examine now, then coordinate with the surgeons.
req2: One IV line and an oral fluid challenge
Suspected post-operative haemorrhage needs two large bore lines and bloods.
Send her to CT before taking bloods
Bedside ultrasound in resus is faster and safer in an unstable patient.
req3: Run 3 litres of crystalloid to correct the pressure
Crystalloid dilutes clotting factors. Give blood products and tranexamic acid.
Give enoxaparin for VTE prophylaxis now
Anticoagulation with active bleeding is dangerous. Delay prophylaxis until haemostasis.
req4: Aspirate the haematoma at the bedside and send her home
An expanding haematoma with shock needs theatre for evacuation and haemostasis.
Observe overnight and transfuse as needed
She is a transient responder. She needs definitive surgical haemostasis.
req5: Start full dose anticoagulation immediately after theatre
Bleeding risk is high in the early post-operative period. Delay prophylaxis until haemostasis is secure.
Do not report the incident, it might upset the clinic
Same-day discharge, drain removal and telephone advice contributed to harm. Formal reporting improves safety.

req1: Nasal cannula at 2 L/min to avoid hyperoxia
She is breathless and confused. Give high flow oxygen and look for the classic signs.
Lumbar puncture for the confusion
The triad of hypoxia, confusion and petechiae after liposuction points to fat embolism. LP is not the first step.
req2: Diagnose fat embolism and skip further tests
Fat embolism is a diagnosis of exclusion. PE, local anaesthetic toxicity and sepsis are treatable mimics.
Start thrombolysis empirically for presumed PE
Thrombolysis without confirmation carries major bleeding risk. Exclude the mimics first.
req3: High dose methylprednisolone as treatment
Steroids are not proven as treatment for established fat embolism. Management is supportive.
Full dose heparin for the embolism
Heparin does not treat fat emboli and increases bleeding risk. Management is supportive.
req4: Ventilate with high tidal volumes to recruit the lungs
High tidal volumes cause lung injury. Use 6 mL/kg predicted body weight.
Admit to the general ward on oxygen
Progressive hypoxaemia needs ICU with lung protective ventilation.
req5: Report nothing, this was a known complication
Large volume aspirate in one session and early discharge are modifiable risks. Report and recommend changes.
Recommend banning liposuction entirely
The evidence supports staged procedures above about 4 litres and overnight observation, not a ban.

req1: Finish the VIP admission paperwork first
Chest pain needs an ECG within 10 minutes wherever the patient is. Paperwork can wait.
Wait for the private cardiologist to arrive
Delay costs myocardium. Get the ECG now.
req2: Wait for the troponin before calling the cath lab
ST elevation on ECG is enough. Troponin rises later and should never delay activation.
Give thrombolysis even though PCI is available within 90 minutes
Primary PCI is preferred when it can be done promptly. Activate the cath lab.
req3: Sublingual nitroglycerin for the chest pain
In right ventricular infarction, nitrates drop preload and can cause profound hypotension.
Morphine 10 mg IV for the pain
Morphine causes venodilation and hypotension in a preload dependent right ventricle.
req4: Admit to CCU and do PCI tomorrow morning
This is a STEMI. Primary PCI should happen now, with door to balloon under 90 minutes.
Treat medically, he is too important to risk the procedure
Status does not change indications. Primary PCI saves myocardium and life.
req5: Discharge on aspirin alone
Post-PCI care needs dual antiplatelet therapy, statin and secondary prevention.
Skip the incident report, nobody was harmed
The VIP pathway delayed the ECG. Reporting system failures prevents future harm.

req1: Book the MRI first, then take the history
A proper history and examination come first and often answer the question.
Refuse to see him because it is not an emergency
He still deserves an assessment for red flags before redirection.
req2: Order the whole-body MRI because he is paying
Unindicated screening finds incidental findings that lead to harmful cascades. Payment does not change that.
Order CA 19-9 as a compromise
Tumour markers are not screening tests and have many false positives. Explain why instead.
req3: Prescribe sleeping tablets for the poor sleep
Hypnotics carry risks. Address reflux, meal timing and alcohol first.
Ignore his symptoms, they are just anxiety
He has real reflux symptoms that deserve treatment.
req4: Tell him to return to the emergency department next week for a repeat check
Screening belongs in primary care or a screening clinic, not the emergency department.
Offer pancreatic cancer screening by ultrasound
There is no evidence for population pancreatic screening. Offer evidence based screening like colorectal.

req1: Examine him repeatedly to monitor the spasms
Touch, light and noise trigger spasms. Minimise stimulation and cluster care.
Keep him in the main resuscitation bay for observation
The noisy resus bay triggers spasms. Move him to a dark, quiet room.
req2: Wait until he needs intubation
Laryngospasm can be sudden and fatal. Secure the airway early and electively.
Attempt awake fibreoptic intubation
Airway manipulation in an awake tetanus patient triggers laryngospasm. Intubate under anaesthesia.
req3: Tetanus toxoid only
Toxoid does not neutralise circulating toxin. Give human tetanus immunoglobulin too.
Skip antibiotics, the toxin is already circulating
Antibiotics eradicate the organism that keeps producing toxin in the wound. Give metronidazole alongside immunoglobulin and debridement.
req4: Low dose diazepam as needed
Generalised tetanus usually needs high dose continuous benzodiazepines plus magnesium.
Suxamethonium infusion for spasm control
Suxamethonium can cause hyperkalaemia. Use benzodiazepines, magnesium and non-depolarising blockers.
req5: Treat hypertension with high dose labetalol infusion
Autonomic instability swings rapidly. Long acting agents can cause profound hypotension. Use magnesium and short acting drugs.
Plan discharge in a week once spasms settle
Tetanus has a long course with autonomic storms. He needs prolonged ICU care.

req1: Treat it as a hangover with IV fluids and antiemetics
Visual loss with a severe anion gap acidosis after home spirits is methanol poisoning until proven otherwise.
Wait for a serum methanol level
Methanol levels are rarely available quickly. Diagnose on anion gap, osmolar gap and visual signs.
req2: Wait for confirmation before blocking alcohol dehydrogenase
Formic acid causes the blindness and acidosis. Block alcohol dehydrogenase immediately.
Give activated charcoal
Charcoal does not bind alcohols. Use fomepizole or ethanol.
req3: Withhold bicarbonate to avoid fluid overload
Correcting acidosis reduces formic acid entry into tissues and the brain. Give bicarbonate.
Give thiamine only
Folinic acid helps metabolise formic acid in methanol poisoning. Give it alongside bicarbonate.
req4: Stop fomepizole once dialysis starts
Methanol keeps being metabolised. Continue the alcohol dehydrogenase blocker during dialysis.
Observe and repeat the gas in 6 hours
Visual loss and severe acidosis are indications for urgent haemodialysis.
req5: Treat him and say nothing about the source
Others may have drunk the same batch. Notify the district health office.
Stop dialysis once he can see a little
Continue dialysis until the anion gap normalises.

req1: Assume it is glyphosate and reassure the family
Blue-green unlabelled herbicide needs identification. The urine dithionite test confirms paraquat quickly.
Wait for a lab paraquat level before acting
The bedside dithionite test gives a quick answer and guides prognosis now.
req2: High flow oxygen to protect her lungs
Oxygen accelerates paraquat lung injury through free radicals. Withhold unless saturations fall below 90%.
Intubate early for airway protection
She is protecting her own airway. Early intubation adds oxygen exposure without benefit.
req3: Induce vomiting with ipecac
Induced vomiting adds oesophageal injury and aspiration risk without benefit.
Withhold analgesia so she can report symptoms
Oropharyngeal burns are very painful. Analgesia is part of supportive care.
req4: Delay psychiatry until she is medically stable
She may lose capacity as she deteriorates. Involve psychiatry and palliative care early while she can participate.
Refer to psychiatry only, palliative care is premature
The prognosis is grave. Early palliative care improves symptom control alongside full care.
req5: Give high flow oxygen for the breathlessness
Oxygen accelerates lung fibrosis. Use opioids and anxiolytics for dyspnoea and discuss goals of care.
Escalate to ECMO and lung transplant listing
Paraquat lung fibrosis rarely responds to such escalation. Discuss a ceiling of treatment with her and the family.

req1: Abdominal ultrasound before anything else
He is lethargic and shocked. Resuscitation and glucose come first.
Oral rehydration solution by bottle
He is lethargic and may need theatre. IV or IO access and nil by mouth.
req2: Attempt the air enema immediately to save time
Reduction in a shocked child risks perforation and collapse. Resuscitate first.
Fluid restrict to 1/2 maintenance
He is in shock and needs bolus resuscitation.
req3: CT abdomen to confirm intussusception
Ultrasound is the diagnostic test of choice and avoids radiation.
Skip imaging and go straight to air enema
Confirm with ultrasound and exclude perforation with a plain film first.
req4: Barium enema without a surgeon present
Air enema is preferred, and a surgical team should be present in case of perforation.
Laparotomy as the first approach
Radiological reduction succeeds in most cases. Surgery is for failure or perforation.
req5: Discharge 2 hours after successful reduction
Recurrence is commonest in the first 24 hours. Admit for observation.
Keep nil by mouth for 3 days
Feeding can resume gradually after successful reduction.

req1: Deep nasopharyngeal suction every hour
Aggressive deep suction causes oedema and trauma. Use gentle nasal suction.
Oxygen to target 100% saturation
Targets of 92% or above are enough. Higher targets prolong admission.
req2: Wait and see if he improves overnight
Apnoea and exhaustion are indications to escalate support now.
Intubate immediately
High flow nasal cannula, then CPAP, often avoids intubation. Escalate stepwise.
req3: Hypotonic IV fluid at full maintenance
Bronchiolitis causes ADH excess. Hypotonic fluid at full rate risks hyponatraemia. Use isotonic at two thirds.
Continue bottle feeds despite his breathing
He is working hard and has apnoea. Oral feeding risks aspiration. Use nasogastric or IV.
req4: Nebulised salbutamol every 4 hours
Bronchodilators do not improve outcomes in bronchiolitis.
Oral prednisolone for 3 days
Steroids do not help bronchiolitis.
req5: Discharge home on oxygen
He has had apnoeas and needs high flow. Admit with clear escalation criteria.
Admit without isolation
RSV spreads easily. Use contact and droplet precautions.

req1: Wait for blood test results to confirm infection
Neonatal sepsis is treated on suspicion. Delay increases mortality.
Lumbar puncture before glucose or access
Glucose and access come first. LP can wait until he is stable.
req2: 50% dextrose bolus
50% dextrose is too concentrated for neonates and damages veins. Use 10% dextrose.
Oral sugar water
He is floppy and not feeding. Hypoglycaemia needs IV dextrose.
req3: Ceftriaxone alone
Ceftriaxone displaces bilirubin and interacts with calcium in neonates, and lacks Listeria cover. Use ampicillin plus cefotaxime.
Oral amoxicillin and outpatient review
A septic neonate needs IV antibiotics at meningitic doses.
req4: Give 60 mL/kg of fluid without reassessing
Neonates overload quickly. Reassess after every bolus for hepatomegaly and crackles.
Withhold inotropes until a central line is in
Inotropes can start peripherally or by IO while central access is obtained.
req5: Stop antibiotics at 48 hours if cultures are negative
With meningitis, GBS needs 14 to 21 days of IV antibiotics.
Discharge after 7 days of oral antibiotics
GBS meningitis needs extended IV therapy and neurodevelopmental follow-up.

req1: Restrain her firmly to stop the seizure
Restraint causes injury. Use left lateral tilt, protect from harm and secure the airway.
Lay her flat on her back
Supine position compresses the vena cava. Use left lateral tilt.
req2: Diazepam IV for the seizure
Magnesium sulphate is superior to diazepam for preventing recurrent eclamptic seizures.
Phenytoin loading dose
Magnesium sulphate is the drug of choice in eclampsia, not phenytoin.
req3: Drop the blood pressure to 110/70 quickly
Rapid lowering reduces placental perfusion and harms the fetus. Target a gradual reduction.
Sublingual nifedipine capsule bitten
Biting the capsule causes unpredictable rapid falls in pressure. Use labetalol, hydralazine or oral nifedipine.
req4: Generous IV fluids to improve placental flow
Pre-eclampsia has leaky capillaries. Excess fluid causes pulmonary oedema. Restrict to 80 mL/h.
Skip steroids because delivery is imminent
At 34 weeks, steroids improve neonatal lung maturity. Give them if time allows.
req5: Continue the pregnancy to 37 weeks with monitoring
Eclampsia is an indication for delivery once the mother is stabilised.
Stop magnesium right after delivery
Seizure risk continues postpartum. Continue magnesium for 24 hours.

req1: Continue the oxytocin infusion
She is collapsing. Call the emergency teams, tilt left and support the airway.
Lay her flat for CPR now
She still has output. Displace the uterus to the left to relieve caval compression.
req2: Prepare to transfer to theatre for caesarean if she arrests
Perimortem caesarean happens where she arrests, within 4 minutes. Have a scalpel at the bedside.
Wait 15 minutes of CPR before delivery
Delivery within 4 to 5 minutes of arrest improves maternal and fetal survival.
req3: 2 litres of fluid rapidly for hypotension
The right ventricle is failing. Fluid overload worsens it. Use vasopressors and inotropes.
Give heparin for presumed pulmonary embolism
This is amniotic fluid embolism with DIC risk. Heparin will worsen bleeding.
req4: Red cells only
Amniotic fluid embolism causes DIC with fibrinogen consumption. Give cryoprecipitate or fibrinogen early.
Wait for coagulation results before blood products
DIC develops fast. Activate massive transfusion now.
req5: Transfer to the general ward after delivery
She survived arrest with ongoing bleeding. She needs ICU and haemostasis.
Stop transfusion once she is in ICU
Continue product guided transfusion while bleeding persists.
